definition: The drawing of a sound's amplitude over time.
A picture of how a sound's frequency content changes over time: time across, frequency up, level as colour.
A frequency scale spaced as pitch is heard: roughly linear below 1 kHz and logarithmic above.
The moving line that marks the current playback position.
avoid: cursor (in docs, keep "playhead" for the moving line)

definition: The position where editing and playback start, set by clicking.
Samples per second of a digital sound, in Hz.
Bits per sample of a digital sound; sets its resolution.
One signal of a sound file; stereo has two.
One channel.
Two channels, left and right.
Stereo written as the sum (mid) and the difference (side) of the channels.
Where in its cycle a wave is at a given moment.
Whether a signal is upright or inverted.
avoid: phase (when the signal is simply inverted)

definition: How strong a signal is, usually in dB.
A change of level, in dB.
The largest absolute sample value.
The peak of the signal between samples, as a DAC would reproduce it.
How loud a sound is heard, as opposed to its level.
Loudness units relative to full scale (ITU-R BS.1770); 1 LU is 1 dB.
The frequency weighting that loudness meters apply before measuring.
Set a sound's peak or loudness to a target.
A gradual change of level at the start (fade-in) or end (fade-out).
Distortion when a signal exceeds the largest value that can be stored.
A constant shift of the signal away from zero.
The level of the background noise under a sound.
A stretch with no sound above the noise floor.
A sound that ends before its decay has died away.
One recorded or rendered version of a sound.
Compute a processed sound and write it as audio.
A sound that repeats without an audible join.
A fade-out of one sound overlapping a fade-in of another.
Cut a sound into parts at chosen points.
Change a sound's duration without changing its pitch.
Change a sound's pitch without changing its duration.
The unit of loudness as heard; 1 sone is the loudness of a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB SPL.
How much a sound's energy sits at high frequencies, as heard; in acum.
The rasping quality of fast amplitude modulation (about 15–300 Hz); in asper.
The sensation of slow amplitude modulation (about 1–20 Hz, strongest near 4 Hz); in vacil.
Zwicker's combination of loudness, sharpness, roughness and fluctuation strength into one annoyance value.
One sound making another harder or impossible to hear.
The frequency range the ear integrates as one; on the Bark scale.
A value drawn over time along the waveform.
A small picture of a whole sound used to find one's way in it.
The overview of one sound as Playhead draws it: waveform, curves and marks in one band.
avoid: lane (a lane is part of a strip)

definition: A named way to draw a strip, written as a short code of layers.
avoid: skin, theme (a theme sets colours only)

definition: The short text that defines a look, for example "form:overlay,shape:mirror,lane:harshness".
One element of a look: a waveform, spectrogram, curve, set of marks or sections.
A horizontal band of a strip that holds one curve.
Curves drawn in one shared band instead of separate lanes.
Drawn symmetrically above and below a centre line, like a waveform.
Drawn upwards from the bottom of the band.
A compact chart that folds a curve into coloured bands of increasing intensity.
A waveform whose height follows a curve, for example perceived loudness, instead of the peak level.
The ordinary peak waveform drawn as a thin line behind another layer.
Ticks along the strip at events, onsets, beats or section boundaries.
The text that says what each colour and line of a strip shows.
How much Playhead analyses: fast (curves only), sound effect, or music.
A number or curve computed from a sound that describes one of its properties.
A descriptor used as input to a classifier or search.
How much is happening: spectral change and the density of events.
How exciting or calming a sound is, after the psychological dimension of the same name.
How unpleasant a sound is to listen to, computed from psychoacoustic annoyance; not the same as roughness.
avoid: roughness, sharpness (both are inputs, not synonyms)

definition: Build-up and release over time, after the model of musical tension by Farbood (2012).
How far the harmony is from rest, from the tonal interval space.
How much a moment differs from what came before.
Change of the spectrum that loudness does not explain.
avoid: novelty (novelty also includes level changes)

definition: Information content of an event: the less expected, the higher.
Where a piece moves to a new part, signed: up where sound enters, down where it falls away or breaks off.
How clearly a regular pulse is felt at each moment.
avoid: beat strength

definition: The moment a sound or note begins.
How strongly new sound arrives at each moment; peaks are hits.
One distinct sound within a file, such as a hit, a step or a creak, with a start and an end.
The first part of a sound, from its start to its peak.
The sustained, often tonal, part of a sound after its attack.
The part of a sound in which it dies away.
The late part of a decay, including reverberation.
A short, fast change of level and spectrum, typically at an attack.
The regular pulse a listener taps along to.
The first beat of a bar.
A group of beats, usually four.
avoid: measure (US)

definition: The speed of the beat, in beats per minute (BPM).
A part of a piece, such as an intro or chorus, found from where its sound changes.
How much a sound returns to states it has been in before.
How often a pattern repeats, in Hz.
How strongly a sound is periodic (pitched) rather than noisy.
How steadily a sound's phases advance; 1 for a steady tone, near 0 for noise.
How much a sound changes when played backwards; high for hits that decay.
avoid: time irreversibility (technical term, docs only)

definition: How much a sound consists of clicks, cracks and crackle, from spectral kurtosis.
avoid: spikiness

definition: A statistic that is 0 for steady noise, −1 for a steady tone and large for clicks.
How fast the spectrum's centre moves up or down, in octaves per second.
The centre of mass of a spectrum; a measure of brightness.
Spectral change that does not move the centre, as when a spectrum spreads or narrows.
Whether events come regularly (below 0), at random (0) or in bursts (above 0).
How evenly a sound's energy is spread over time.
The time a sound takes to fall by 60 dB.
How quickly a vibrating body loses energy.
What an impacted object is made of, as heard: damped, glass-like or metal-like.
One frequency component of a sound.
A partial above the lowest one.
With partials that are not whole-number multiples of a fundamental, as in bells and struck metal.
Automatic checks for clipping, DC offset, silence and cut tails.
A test that edits a sound in a known way and checks that the analysis changes as it must.
avoid: unit test

definition: A tool that turns down resonances only while the sound is harsh.
avoid: de-esser (a de-esser keys on level in one band)

definition: A tool that splits a sound into its transient part and its sustained part, to rebalance them.
avoid: transient shaper (works on level, not on a split)

definition: A tool that separates a sound into layers and mixes them again at new levels.
A tool that turns the tension curve into gain and brightness automation.
A tool that finds and crossfades loop points where the sound repeats best.
Several slightly different versions of one sound, to avoid repetition in games.
A tool that repairs what the quality checks flag before a sound is exported.
Reverberation fed only from the decays of the events, keeping the attacks dry.
Saturation applied only to the events' attacks or bodies.
A tool that lengthens or shortens how long each event rings after its peak.
A tool that evens out how loud the events are, one gain per event, without touching their shape.
avoid: compress (a compressor changes the shape)

definition: Turn stereo into mono with the channels' phase lined up, so nothing cancels.
avoid: sum to mono (the plain sum)

definition: Make or widen stereo only after the attacks, keeping attacks centred and the result mono-compatible.
Turn more channels into fewer.
How well a stereo sound survives being summed to mono.
Making two signals less alike while keeping their spectrum, to widen a stereo image.
Regular notches in a spectrum when a signal is summed with a delayed copy of itself.
Loss of level when signals of opposite phase are summed.
A faint smear of a sound before its attack, caused by frame-based processing.
An equaliser: a filter that changes the level of frequency bands.
An EQ whose band gains follow the level in each band.
Parameter changes over time, recorded or drawn.
A processor that turns loud passages down by a ratio above a threshold.
The level above which a processor acts.
How strongly a compressor turns the level down above its threshold.
How fast a processor reacts when the level rises.
How fast a processor recovers when the level falls.
A processor or condition that opens only above a threshold.
Soft distortion that adds harmonics and rounds peaks.
Audible rise and fall of the background caused by a compressor.
How alike the events are in loudness.
Effects applied one after another to a sound.
A saved set of settings.
A gradual blend from one sound into another.
Combining the spectrum of one sound with the envelope or excitation of another.
Filtering one sound by another, for example by a room's impulse response.
Giving one sound the level envelope of another.
Multiplying two signals, which creates sum and difference frequencies.
Built from many short grains of sound.
A short added sound placed at a moment of another sound to emphasise it.
A part of the app that makes new sounds from parameters.
A sound generator built from oscillators, noise, envelopes and filters.
A physical model of a struck object of a given material and shape.
Rebuilding a sound from parameters measured on it, such as its partials and decays.
Made of resonant modes, each with a frequency and a decay.
A continuous sound made of many small events, such as rain, fire or gravel.
A generator in which an action, such as an object moving or a force, drives the sound of a medium that responds to it (gravel, water, air).
What reacts to an action: gravel, leaves, water, air, sparks or a force field.
A curve that controls a sound's parameters over time.
How slowly a reaction settles after the action stops.
Everyday sounds performed and recorded in sync with picture.
The background sound of a place.
A short sound played once, such as a hit or a UI click.
The sound of something moving fast past the listener.
The last steps before export: format, channels, fades and level.
A long solid body, such as a rod or beam.
A thin flat body.
A stretched skin, as on a drum.
A thin curved body, such as a can or pot.
A stiff string or wire that rings with slightly stretched (inharmonic) partials.
A hollow body with flat sides.
A row of a DAW session that holds clips on the timeline and has its own mixer channel.
avoid: lane (a band inside a strip); channel (one signal of a sound file)

definition: A track that holds other tracks: it sums their sound and can show them as one.
avoid: group (a mixer group or VCA)

definition: One piece of audio or MIDI on a track, placed at a point in time.
avoid: event (here a sound event the analysis finds; Cubase calls clips events); region (here a named span of time; Logic calls clips regions); item (REAPER's word, fine in REAPER-only texts)

definition: All of one piece of DAW work: its tracks, clips, routing and settings; also called a project.
The time axis of a session, along which clips are placed.
A named point in time stored in a session or a sound file (a cue in a WAV file).
avoid: marks (the ticks Playhead draws on a strip; a marker is what an editor stores)

definition: A named span of time with a start and an end, stored in a session or a sound file.
Making a clip or an edit jump to the nearest grid line, marker, clip edge or onset while it is moved.
Silencing a track without removing it; the button is often labelled M.
Hearing only the soloed tracks; the button is often labelled S.
The level control of a mixer channel.
Where a sound sits between left and right; also the control that sets it.
A mixer channel that sums the signals sent to it, so they can be processed together (a drum bus, a reverb bus).
The bus everything is summed into before the output: what is rendered as the mix.
A copy of a track's signal sent to a bus at its own level, while the track keeps playing.
An effect in a channel's own signal path, which all of the signal passes through.
How signals travel between tracks, buses, sends and outputs.
The sum of all tracks as it is heard; also the work of balancing them.
A submix of related tracks (drums, dialogue, music) rendered to its own file, so the parts can be mixed or delivered separately.
A point where the waveform crosses zero; cuts and loop points made there do not click.
The distance in dB between the highest level a signal reaches and the level where it would clip.
The span in dB between a sound's loud and quiet parts, or between the highest level a system takes and its noise floor.
avoid: loudness range (a loudness measure, in LU)

definition: How much the loudness of a programme varies, in LU: the span between the 10th and 95th percentile of its short-term loudness.
avoid: dynamic range (a level measure, in dB)

definition: The loudness of a whole programme, with silence and quiet passages gated out, in LUFS.
Loudness over a sliding 3 s window, in LUFS.
Loudness over a sliding 400 ms window, in LUFS.
The integrated loudness a programme is delivered or played at, such as −23 LUFS for EBU R 128 broadcast or about −14 LUFS on streaming services.
Bringing two versions to the same loudness before comparing them, so that the louder one does not seem better only because it is louder.
Switching between two versions, ideally at matched loudness, to hear which is better.
A finished recording played for comparison while mixing or mastering.
The ratio of peak to RMS level, in dB: high for punchy, dynamic sound, low for dense, compressed sound.
The root mean square of a signal over a window: its average power, as a level.
How different the two channels are, from mono (not at all) to wide.
How a quantity, usually level, changes over the course of a sound; also a drawn curve that controls a parameter.
A range of frequencies measured or processed together: an EQ band, a critical band, a mel band.
A filter that passes the frequencies above its cutoff and attenuates those below.
avoid: low-cut (the same filter; use one term)

definition: A filter that passes the frequencies below its cutoff and attenuates those above.
avoid: high-cut (the same filter; use one term)

definition: A compressor with a very high ratio and a fast attack that keeps the level below a ceiling.
A compressor that works on several frequency bands separately.
A processor that raises or lowers the attack and the sustain of sounds independently of their level.
A second input through which another signal controls a processor, as when music is turned down under dialogue.
Turning one sound down automatically while another plays, usually with a sidechained compressor.
The dense reflections of a sound in a space, or an effect that imitates them.
An effect that plays the sound again after a set time, often repeating and fading (echo).
Low-level noise added when the bit depth is reduced, so that the rounding error becomes noise instead of distortion.
The last stage before release: the final EQ, dynamics and loudness of a mix, and checks for the delivery format.
The moment in a dance track when the full beat and bass come in, usually after a build-up or a breakdown.
avoid: drop for a fall in level (Playhead says fall or break)

definition: A passage that raises tension towards a drop: rising pitch, filter sweeps, faster rolls, a riser.
A passage where the beat and bass fall away, leaving pads, chords or vocals.
A sound that rises in pitch, brightness or level to lead into a drop or a transition.
A glide through a range of frequencies: a tone or noise whose pitch or brightness moves, or a filter swept across the spectrum.
A stored position in a track that a DJ or a player jumps to or starts from.
The beats and bars of a track as a grid, used to sync, loop and jump in time.
Bringing two tracks to the same tempo with their beats aligned.
A run of bars, usually 8, 16 or 32 in dance music, that forms one musical unit; DJs mix at phrase boundaries.
The tonal centre and scale of a piece, such as A minor; DJs mix tracks in compatible keys (harmonic mixing).
